title: Hymn 4, sound: kaam karodh
hookLine: kaam karodh nagar bahu bhariaa (Gauri Purbi M4, ang 13)

lines: A NEW VOICE: GURU RAM DAS.
A TOWN, AND A CROWDED ONE.
THE FIRST LINE IS A WARNING.
cards: A new voice enters Sohila tonight. The first three hymns were Guru Nanak's. The fourth is by Guru Ram Das, the fourth Guru, whom Sikhs remember as the founder of the town that grew into Amritsar.
Someone who founds a town learns how one fills up, street by street. So it fits that his hymn is about a crowded town. Only this town isn't on any map.
It's a body at the end of a long day, with whatever it's still carrying.

teach.b: Here's the line: kaam karodh nagar bahu bhariaa. Word by word. Kaam: desire that has run out of control, lust, craving.

teach.h: NAGAR: THE CITY OF THE BODY.
teach.b: Nagar: a town, a city. Bahu: very much. Bhariaa: filled.
So: the city is crammed with desire and anger. The city is the body, and the mind that lives in it, its streets full of two restless characters who never seem to sleep.
Then the line finishes, and the warning becomes a hope.
In paraphrase: meeting the holy, they are broken to pieces.

The holy here is saadhoo, the person who has truly given themselves to God, and some readers hear in it the sangat, the company of people who sing God's praise together. So the hymn doesn't pretend the city is quiet.
It names the crowd, and it names what breaks it up. The hymn is in Raag Gauri Purbi, on Ang 13, right after Guru Nanak's three. Listen to its sound: kaam and karodh both open on a hard k.

teach.h: A LINE THAT OPENS WITH A JOLT.
teach.b: The line begins with a jolt, like a door banged at night, hard to sleep through.
Tomorrow, the rest of the city's residents. Today, two loud names, a crowded town, and the promise that the crowd can be broken.

how: This is the fourth of the five hymns Sikhs recite every night in Kirtan Sohila; it is Guru Ram Das's, and it follows the three hymns of Guru Nanak.

o: anger, one of the loud crowd in the body's city
craving, desire that has run out of control
a city crowded with people late at night

games.q: the first line of hymn 4 — tap the pairs.

s: Sohila's fourth hymn is by Guru Nanak
it's by Guru Ram Das, the fourth Guru; the first three are Guru Nanak's.
in the hymn, the city stands for the body
a town crammed with desire and anger.
the hymn says the city can never be cleared
meeting the holy, desire and anger are broken to pieces.

games.q: your city is crammed with desire and anger. what does the hymn's first line say breaks them?
games.why: mil saadhoo: meeting the holy, they are broken to pieces.

practice: Say the line once, clearly, feeling the two hard k sounds: kaam karodh nagar bahu bhariaa.

Then sit and notice, without judging, whether either one is in your city right now, a little irritation, a craving, the way you'd notice a car passing outside. Let your shoulders drop, and if you pray, say Waheguru once.

wordCard.voice: Krodh, anger: Sohila's fourth hymn, by Guru Ram Das, the city of the body is crammed with desire and anger, and meeting the holy, they are broken.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: krodh, anger; sung as karodh in the hymn's first line.

carryVoice: Your line: kaam karodh. Desire and anger, named, and not the last word. Day four hundred thirty.

sources.ref: Gauri Purbi M4, Ang 13 (Kirtan Sohila, hymn 4)
